extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (aesthetics and metaphysics); scholars interested in art, genius, and theory of knowledge
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical criteria for what constitutes art and genius: how art apprehends and communicates eternal Ideas, how genius attains the mode of pure, will-less perception necessary to produce art, and how imagination and perception function in aesthetic creation and appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's aim — communication of Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Art repeats or reproduces the eternal Ideas grasped through pure contemplation; its one aim the communication of this knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art's source is the knowledge of Ideas and its aim is to communicate that knowledge. Unlike science, which traces relations and is useful for the will, art isolates the particular object and makes it representative of the whole (the Idea), thereby conveying the eternal, essential content of phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as the way of viewing independent of the principle of sufficient reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is defined as 'the way of viewing things independent of the principle of sufficient reason', opposed to the method of experience and science, which proceeds according to that principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion distinguishes artistic perception (vertical, contemplative, isolating the Idea) from scientific/rational perception (horizontal, tracing relations). Art pauses time and relations to present the essential; science continually extends and never attains a final goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate objectivity — art apprehends the Idea, not mere phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The Platonic Idea is the direct and therefore adequate objectivity of the thing-in-itself; art should present the Idea (adequate objectivity) rather than the merely phenomenal, multiplied particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should present the essential, permanent form (Idea) behind transient phenomena. Particular forms and accidental details are unessential to the Idea and are only for the individual observer; art must reveal the essential nature (e.g., laws manifesting in clouds, brooks, crystals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as the faculty of pure, will-less perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is the capacity to become a 'pure subject of knowledge'—to lose one's individuality and will, ceasing to trace relations and resting in fixed contemplation of the object—so as to grasp Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genius requires temporarily abandoning self-interest and the relations demanded by the principle of sufficient reason. It is the 'completest objectivity' of the mind, allowing sustained, disinterested perception and the ability to reproduce what has been apprehended in lasting artistic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained perception and reproducive capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The man of genius must continue in the state of pure perception for a sufficient length of time and with sufficient consciousness to reproduce by deliberate art what has been apprehended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary glimpses are insufficient; the creative individual must hold the pure perception long enough to fix the 'wavering images' and make them communicable. This endurance of disinterested attention is part of what distinguishes genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination: necessary extension of perception (necessary but not sufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination extends the horizon of the man of genius beyond the limits of his actual personal apperception and is required to construct the whole out of the little that presents itself; extraordinary imagination accompanies and is a necessary condition of genius, but does not by itself indicate genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination allows the genius to see not just what nature actually produced but what it strove to produce (ideal forms behind imperfect instances). However, strong imagination without the capacity for pure, disinterested perception leads to mere fantasy or dreaming, not genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from mere imagination/dreaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Men with much imagination but no genius use imagined objects for egotistic castles-in-the-air and the relations of such phantasies; this makes them dreamers rather than artists of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether imagination serves the apprehension and communication of Ideas (art) or merely the construction of egotistic fictions (novels for entertainment, daydreams). The former contributes to art; the latter does not establish genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art isolates the particular as representative of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Art plucks an object out of the stream of the world's course and makes this particular thing the representative of the whole, an equivalent of the endless multitude in space and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, an artwork focuses on a singular instance but thereby stands for the universal Idea. This is why art 'pauses' time: the particular is elevated to embody the essential, timeless aspect of a species or force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium determined by material — type of Idea reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: According to what the material is in which it reproduces, the knowledge of Ideas becomes sculpture or painting, poetry or music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing art, consider the medium's capacity to render the apprehended Idea: choose forms and techniques appropriate to how the Idea manifests in that material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science vs art: theme and method difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Science treats phenomena—their laws, connections, and relations—proceeding according to the principle of sufficient reason; art treats Ideas (the eternal, essential content) and proceeds by contemplative perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For aesthetic judgement, recognize whether a work aims to map relations (scientific or pragmatic) or to present essential forms and Ideas (art). Their aims, validity, and usefulness differ: science for practical life, art for contemplation and knowledge of Ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of genius in the perceiver/creator's attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The man of genius is distinguished by a glance that is keen and steady, bearing the stamp of perception and contemplation; the ordinary man quickly seeks concepts and relations, has a more superficial or vacant glance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observable differences in how creators/viewers attend to objects (duration, steadiness, depth of gaze) indicate their capacity for disinterested perception; this can be used as a practical indicator when assessing artistic temperament or responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art attains a final goal (completeness) unlike science
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is everywhere at its goal because it presents the Idea in isolation; science, constantly extending along forms of reason and consequence, never reaches final satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess artworks on whether they accomplish their contemplative aim—presenting the Idea fully within the work—whereas scientific or pragmatic inquiries are judged by continual extension and utility rather than final completeness.
